H1.text: A gas stove flame. A burning candle. A tank of petrol. All three run on the same family of molecules.

H2.text: They are alkanes, chains of only carbon and hydrogen. Yet one is a gas, one is a liquid, and one is a solid.

H3.text: Diya sees it in the kitchen. The stove gas floats away into the air, but the candle wax just sits there, solid.

H4.text: Both are made of carbon and hydrogen. So why are they so different?

H5.text: By the end, you will know how alkanes behave, and how they react.

P1.text: So what decides it? Think of cooked noodles.

P2.text: Short noodles slip apart easily. Long noodles tangle and stick together.

P3.text: Alkane molecules are like that. They are non polar, so they hold each other only by weak pulls, called van der Waals forces.

P4.text: A longer chain has more surface to touch its neighbours, so the pulls add up.

P5.text: More pull means more heat is needed to pull them apart. So the boiling point goes up.

P6.text: That is why alkanes with one to four carbons are gases, five to seventeen are liquids, and eighteen or more are solids, at room temperature.

S1.text: Now watch branching on our molecule bench.

S2.text: Here are three molecules with the same formula, C five H twelve.

S3.text: Pentane is one straight chain. It boils at three hundred and nine point one kelvin.

S4.text: Move one carbon to the side, and we get two methyl butane. It boils lower, at three hundred point nine kelvin.

S5.text: Move two carbons, and we get two two dimethyl propane, almost a ball. It boils at only two hundred and eighty two point five kelvin.

S6.text: Why? A ball touches its neighbours at fewer points than a long chain.

S7.text: Less contact, weaker pulls, lower boiling point. Same mass, but the shape decides.

B1.text: One more physical fact. Alkanes do not mix with water.

B2.text: Water is polar, and alkanes are non polar. Like dissolves like, so the two stay apart.

B3.text: Now compare hexane, a straight chain of six carbons, with two two dimethyl butane, also six carbons, but bunched up.

B4.text: Pause and think. Which one boils at a higher temperature?

B5.text: Hexane! Its long chain touches more neighbours. More contact, stronger pull, higher boiling point.

D1.text: Now the chemistry. Alkanes are lazy. But in light, chlorine can replace their hydrogens. This is halogenation. Let's follow it, link by link.

D2.text: Link one, initiation. Light splits a chlorine molecule evenly. Each chlorine atom keeps one electron. An atom with one unpaired electron is called a free radical.

D3.text: Link two. A chlorine radical pulls a hydrogen off methane. It makes hydrogen chloride, and leaves a methyl radical behind.

D4.text: Link three. The methyl radical grabs one chlorine atom from a chlorine molecule. Chloromethane forms, and a new chlorine radical is set free.

D5.text: That new radical starts link two again. One spark keeps a whole chain going. Links two and three are called propagation.

D6.text: Link four, termination. Two radicals meet and pair their electrons. Two methyl radicals can even make ethane. The chain stops.

T1.text: Remember this. Alkanes are lazy, but light, heat or a catalyst wakes them up.

W1.text: Now, one worked example. How much heat do we get by burning eight grams of methane?

W2.text: Step one. Write the balanced equation. Methane plus two oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus two water.

W3.text: Step two. Burning one mole of methane gives out eight hundred and ninety kilojoules. The minus sign means heat leaves.

W4.text: Step three. The molar mass of methane is sixteen grams. So eight grams is half a mole.

W5.text: Step four. Half of eight hundred and ninety is four hundred and forty five kilojoules of heat.

W6.text: This is why alkanes make such good fuels.

C1.text: Alkanes have more tricks. With a catalyst and a limited supply of air, burning stops halfway. This is controlled oxidation. Methane over copper, at five hundred and twenty three kelvin and one hundred atmospheres, gives methanol.

C2.text: Isomerisation. Hexane, heated with aluminium chloride and hydrogen chloride, rearranges into branched chains.

C3.text: Aromatisation. Hexane, at seven hundred and seventy three kelvin, over metal oxides on alumina, closes into a benzene ring.

C4.text: Methane with steam over nickel, at twelve hundred and seventy three kelvin, gives carbon monoxide and hydrogen.

C5.text: And pyrolysis. Strong heat cracks big alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes. Oil gas is made from kerosene this way.

X2.text: Students think the chlorination of methane gives only chloromethane.

X3.text: Wrong. The chain keeps going. With more chlorine, we also get dichloromethane, chloroform and carbon tetrachloride. A mixture.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Board papers ask the free radical steps. Entrance tests ask the boiling point order and the products of reactions.

Q1.text: Exam level now. In the chlorination of methane in light, which step can form ethane? Pause and solve.

A2.text: Initiation only splits chlorine into two chlorine radicals.

A3.text: The two propagation steps make hydrogen chloride and chloromethane, and always leave a radical behind.

A4.text: Only in termination do two methyl radicals meet. They pair their electrons into a carbon carbon bond. That is ethane.
